observation_review.reasoning: Source analysis shows the real pedestal (part-4) appears as a flared metal foot providing stability in display context. The craft prediction that folded-under cardboard edges will sit perfectly flat is questionable: folding adds localized double thickness at corners and depends on crease accuracy. The reported 'actual' is explicitly hypothetical software probe only, not a physical trial, so it cannot verify flatness or rocking. Outcome 'different' therefore reflects a simulated limitation, not proof of user error or model failure.

possible_explanations.explanation: Folded-under edges overlap at corners, creating a thicker high spot that contacts the table first and causes rocking when tapped.
possible_explanations.distinguishing_observation: With base on a known flat table, view underside at eye level toward light and press each edge lightly; see if rocking pivots consistently on one folded corner and light gap is larger there.

possible_explanations.explanation: Cardboard blank is slightly warped or folds are unevenly creased, so the foot is not planar regardless of technique.
possible_explanations.distinguishing_observation: Remove the taped ring and place the square alone on the table, then flip it over; observe if bow direction or rocking point moves with the cardboard rather than the folds.

possible_explanations.explanation: Simulation misinterpreted the taped cardboard ring thickness or placement as base unevenness, which would not occur in a passive visual check.
possible_explanations.distinguishing_observation: Compare stability visually with ring on versus ring lifted off by fingertips, without re-folding; note if rocking reported only in software matches observable gap under real cardboard.

limits: Report is hypothetical-test with no physical trial - not independent verification of materials or construction
Review is interpretation of craft logic only, not inspection of the real GE fan or measurement of its base
Distinguishing observations are passive visual checks on the separate cardboard model only; do not load, electrify, or alter the original object

learning.title: Vintage GE Pedestal Fan - Flared Base Craft Stability Review
learning.answer: This question asks about the separate tabletop craft that models the flared pedestal base (part-4) of the vintage GE table fan. The real fan uses a cast flared foot for tipping resistance, visible as a stable circular base on the display plinth. The craft analogue uses folded cardboard to illustrate stability principles on a small scale. The reported 'different' outcome is from a hypothetical software probe only, not a physical trial, so it is not evidence that a real folded cardboard base would rock or that the technique failed.
safety_notes: Craft uses only paper materials - no blades, electricity, or sharp tools, keep small tape pieces away from young children
Observe passively on a flat table; do not press hard, add weight, or modify the museum object
limitations: This card analogue does not reproduce the weight, rigidity, or cast-metal flatness of the real GE pedestal base
A slowly tapped paper base cannot demonstrate actual fan vibration resistance or tipping loads
Hypothetical software prediction is not a physical test of stability
